title: Design a Notification System
summary: Get the right message to the right person by push, email or SMS. Respect preferences, reserve capacity for urgent messages, switch providers during outages, enforce rate limits, catch duplicates and track delivery.
body:
## Practice first

Design the notification platform a large consumer company uses to reach its users. Product teams (payments, social, security, marketing) call one internal API and say "tell user 42 that their payment failed"; the platform decides which channels to use (mobile push, email, SMS), renders the message in the user's language, respects the user's preferences, delivers through third-party providers and reports what happened.

Take 10 minutes to sketch the requirements, entities, send API and a baseline that delivers a message end to end. Choose two deep dives, then compare your decisions with this walkthrough. This is one design you can defend, not a list of product names to memorize.

## Functional requirements

Core (users of the platform should be able to):

1. **Send a notification**: an internal service submits an event type, one or more recipients (or a saved segment) and template data; the platform delivers it on the right channels.
2. **Control preferences**: end users opt in or out per category and channel (for example "marketing email: off", "security SMS: on") and set quiet hours; the platform honours them on every send.
3. **Track delivery**: senders and support staff can see, per recipient and channel, whether a notification was sent, delivered, failed or opened.

Out of scope: the campaign-builder UI, A/B testing, running our own SMTP servers or SMS carrier connections, the in-app notification inbox UI, and analytics dashboards. We integrate with providers such as APNs, FCM, an email service and an SMS gateway rather than replacing them.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** about 1 billion notifications per day across channels, with 10x bursts during breaking news or a large campaign. Broadcasts can target 50 million users.
- **Latency by priority:** transactional, time-critical messages (one-time passcodes, fraud alerts) reach the provider within 5 seconds at p99, even during a marketing blast. Bulk/marketing may take minutes to hours and must be throttled.
- **Durability over latency on accept:** once the API returns `202 Accepted`, the notification must not be lost. Delivery is at-least-once to providers, with deduplication so users almost never see a duplicate.
- **Availability vs consistency, per operation:** the send API favours availability (99.99%). Preference reads may be a few seconds stale for normal sends, but an opt-out must take effect within about a minute and a user editing their settings must read their own write.
- **Good citizenship:** never exceed provider rate limits, cap how often a single user is notified per category, and never send marketing during quiet hours.

## Back-of-the-envelope

Only the numbers that drive decisions:

- **Throughput:** 1B / 86,400 s ≈ 11,600 sends/s average; a 10x burst is ~116,000/s. That is too much for synchronous provider calls inside a request, and bursty enough that we need a buffer, so **a durable queue between accept and deliver** is mandatory.
- **Broadcast fan-out:** 50M recipients at a sustained 100k deliveries/s takes ~500 s ≈ 8 minutes. A broadcast is therefore a long-running job that must be chunked, resumable and throttled, not one API call that loops.
- **Channel mix and cost:** assume 70% push, 25% email, 5% SMS. 5% of 1B is 50M SMS/day; at roughly a cent per message that is about $500k/day. SMS is the expensive channel, so channel selection and fallback ("push first, SMS only if push is not delivered in 2 minutes") are cost decisions, not just UX.
- **Provider ceilings:** an SMS sender number has a fixed throughput (a US long code manages about one message per second; short codes and toll-free numbers far more), and FCM/APNs/email providers apply per-project or per-account quotas. We need **per-provider token buckets** in the delivery tier.
- **Delivery log size:** each attempt record is ~500 bytes; 1B/day × 500 B ≈ 500 GB/day, ~15 TB for 30 days of retention. That is write-heavy, append-only, time-bounded data: a wide-column store with TTLs fits better than the relational database holding preferences.

## Core entities

- **Notification**: id, idempotency key, sender service, type/category, priority, recipients or segment, template data, scheduled time.
- **Template**: type × channel × locale × version; channel-specific body (push title/body, email subject/HTML, SMS text).
- **Preference**: user, category, channel, enabled, quiet hours and time zone.
- **Contact point**: user, channel, address (device token, email, phone), verified flag, last seen.
- **Delivery**: notification id, user, channel, provider, status, provider message id, timestamps.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    NOTIFICATION ||--o{ DELIVERY : "fans out to"
    TEMPLATE ||--o{ NOTIFICATION : renders
    USER ||--o{ PREFERENCE : sets
    USER ||--o{ CONTACT_POINT : owns
    USER ||--o{ DELIVERY : receives
    CONTACT_POINT ||--o{ DELIVERY : "addressed to"
```

A notification says what the sender wants to communicate. A delivery tracks an attempt to reach one user on one channel. That split lets one request become 50 million deliveries, each with its own status, retries and provider ID.

## API

Internal sender API (service-to-service auth, for example mTLS plus a per-service allow-list of categories it may send):

```text
POST /v1/notifications
Idempotency-Key: payments-evt-88231
{
  "type": "payment_failed",          // maps to category + templates
  "recipients": { "userIds": ["u_42"] },   // or { "segmentId": "seg_9" }
  "data": { "amount": "12.50", "merchant": "Acme" },
  "priority": "transactional",       // transactional | standard | bulk
  "sendAt": null                     // optional schedule
}
-> 202 { "notificationId": "n_7f3", "status": "accepted" }

GET /v1/notifications/n_7f3/deliveries?cursor=...&limit=100
-> 200 { "items": [ { "userId": "u_42", "channel": "push",
                      "status": "delivered", "updatedAt": "..." } ],
         "nextCursor": "..." }
```

End-user API (user session auth):

```text
GET  /v1/me/preferences
PUT  /v1/me/preferences          { "category": "marketing", "channel": "email", "enabled": false }
POST /v1/me/devices              { "platform": "ios", "token": "..." }
```

Provider callbacks (signature verified per provider): `POST /v1/webhooks/{provider}` for delivery receipts, bounces and unsubscribes.

`202` rather than `200` is deliberate: the API promises durable acceptance, not delivery. The idempotency key makes the sender's retries safe.

## High-level design

Build it one requirement at a time.

**Send a notification.** The Notification API authenticates the caller, validates the type, records the idempotency key and the request in its database, and publishes a message to a Kafka topic chosen by priority. A **fan-out worker** expands recipients (a segment becomes millions of user ids, processed in chunks), and for each user loads preferences and contact points, picks channels, renders the template for the user's locale and emits one job per (user, channel) to a channel queue. **Channel workers** (push, email, SMS) pull jobs, apply per-provider rate limits and call the provider.

**Control preferences.** A Preference service owns preferences and contact points in a relational database (small rows, strong consistency for the user's own edits) fronted by a cache that fan-out workers read.

**Track delivery.** Channel workers write an attempt record when they hand off to a provider. Providers report back later through webhooks (APNs and FCM return errors synchronously; email and SMS providers send delivery and bounce events asynchronously). A status ingester writes those into the delivery log, which the status API reads.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S["Internal services"] --> API["Notification API"]
    API --> NDB[("Requests DB")]
    API --> TQ[["Topics by priority"]]
    TQ --> FO["Fan-out and render workers"]
    FO --> PS["Preference service"]
    PS --> PDB[("Prefs and contacts")]
    FO --> CQ[["Channel queues"]]
    CQ --> CW["Push, email, SMS workers"]
    CW --> PR["Providers: APNs, FCM, email, SMS"]
    PR --> WH["Webhook ingester"]
    CW --> DL[("Delivery log")]
    WH --> DL
```

Walk an OTP through it. The auth service posts `type=login_otp, priority=transactional` with an idempotency key. The API stores the request and publishes to the transactional topic, then returns 202 in tens of milliseconds. A fan-out worker reads it, sees the category is "security" (cannot be disabled, ignores quiet hours), finds a verified phone number, renders the SMS template in Spanish and enqueues an SMS job. The SMS worker takes a token from the provider's bucket, calls the SMS gateway, records `sent` with the provider's message id, and a few seconds later the gateway's webhook flips the record to `delivered`.

## Deep dives

### 1. Never lose an accepted notification (durability and provider failure)

**Problem:** providers time out, return 5xx and sometimes disappear for an hour. Workers crash mid-batch too. A 202 promises durable acceptance and continued processing, not guaranteed delivery: invalid addresses, exhausted retries and a dead-letter queue can still end without delivery.

- **Bad: call the provider inside the API request.** Latency and availability become the provider's; a provider outage turns into failed sends upstream and retry storms from every caller.
- **Good: persist, queue, retry.** The API writes the request and enqueues it (using a transactional outbox, or simply treating the Kafka write as the commit point and returning 202 only after an acknowledged write with `acks=all`). Workers commit their queue offset only after the delivery record is written. Failed provider calls retry with exponential backoff and jitter; after N attempts the job goes to a dead-letter queue with the error for inspection and replay.
- **Great: add per-provider circuit breakers and failover.** For email and SMS, contract two providers. Each channel worker tracks error rate and latency per provider; when the breaker opens, traffic shifts to the secondary until health checks pass. Push has no alternative path (APNs is the only way to reach an iPhone), so for push the right response is to retry with backoff and, for transactional messages, fall back to a different channel.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant W as SMS worker
    participant CB as Circuit breaker
    participant P1 as Primary SMS provider
    participant P2 as Secondary SMS provider
    participant DL as Delivery log
    W->>CB: Primary healthy?
    CB-->>W: Yes
    W->>P1: Send OTP, timeout 2s
    P1-->>W: Timeout
    W->>CB: Record failure, breaker opens
    W->>P2: Retry with same delivery id
    P2-->>W: Accepted, msg id m9
    W->>DL: Status sent via P2, msg id m9
```

The worker sends with a short timeout. When the primary times out and the failure rate crosses the threshold, the breaker opens and the retry goes to the secondary using the *same* delivery id, so the dedupe check in deep dive 3 still applies. The delivery log records which provider actually sent it, which matters when its webhook arrives later. Note the residual risk: the primary may have delivered the message despite timing out, so a failover can produce a duplicate SMS. For OTPs that is acceptable (the code is the same); for a "payment received" text it is a product decision worth stating.

**Recommendation:** queue plus bounded retries plus DLQ is the baseline; per-provider breakers and secondary providers for email/SMS are what make the 99.99% target credible.

### 2. OTPs must not wait behind a 50M-user campaign (priority and isolation)

**Problem:** a marketing broadcast enqueues 50M jobs. If an OTP lands behind them in the same queue, it waits eight minutes and the user gives up logging in.

- **Bad: one FIFO queue with a priority field.** Kafka and most log-based queues have no priority reordering; consumers see messages in partition order, so a field does nothing.
- **Good: separate topics per priority** with separate consumer groups. Transactional traffic never shares a partition with bulk.
- **Great: separate topics and reserved capacity at every shared resource.** Priority isolation fails at the narrowest shared point, which is usually the provider quota. Give transactional traffic its own worker pool and its own share of each provider's token bucket (for example 30% reserved, unused share borrowable), and pace bulk sends with an explicit rate so a campaign drains at a planned speed instead of as fast as possible.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    API["Notification API"] --> T1[["Transactional topic"]]
    API --> T2[["Standard topic"]]
    API --> T3[["Bulk topic"]]
    T1 --> W1["Worker pool A, always on"]
    T2 --> W2["Worker pool B"]
    T3 --> W3["Worker pool C, paced"]
    W1 --> RL["Per-provider token buckets"]
    W2 --> RL
    W3 --> RL
    RL --> PR["Providers"]
```

Each priority has its own topic and worker pool, so a backlog in bulk does not delay transactional consumption. All pools meet at the per-provider token buckets, which is why those buckets must reserve capacity for the transactional class rather than being first come, first served. Bulk workers also read a pacing rate (deliveries per second per campaign) so operators can slow or pause a campaign without touching other traffic.

Large segments are expanded by a **chunked fan-out job**: the segment is split into ranges of user ids, each range is a task with a checkpoint, and a crashed worker resumes from the last completed chunk. This is the long-running-task pattern; it also lets you cancel a campaign halfway.

### 3. Do not notify the same user twice (idempotency and dedupe)

**Problem:** duplicates come from four places: the sender retries a POST, Kafka redelivers after a consumer crash, a provider call times out but succeeded, and two different upstream events describe the same real-world fact.

- **Bad: hope for exactly-once delivery from the queue.** Even with transactional Kafka, the provider call is an external side effect outside the transaction.
- **Good: idempotency at each boundary.** The API stores `(sender, idempotency_key)` with a unique constraint and returns the original notification id on a repeat. Each delivery gets a deterministic id, `hash(notification_id, user_id, channel)`, so a redelivered job maps to the same record.
- **Great: claim before calling, and use provider features.** Before calling the provider, the worker atomically claims the delivery id (for example `SET delivery:{id} sending NX EX 86400` in Redis, or a conditional insert in the delivery log). If the claim exists with status `sent`, skip. Pass collapse identifiers where providers support them (`apns-collapse-id`, FCM `collapse_key`) so the device shows one notification even if two arrive. For semantic duplicates, add a content-level rule such as "at most one `cart_reminder` per user per 24 hours", enforced with a per-user counter.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as Channel queue
    participant W as Push worker
    participant R as Dedupe store
    participant P as Push provider
    K->>W: Job d1, attempt 2 after crash
    W->>R: Claim d1 if absent
    R-->>W: Already sent
    W->>K: Commit offset, skip send
    K->>W: Job d2, first attempt
    W->>R: Claim d2 if absent
    R-->>W: Claimed
    W->>P: Send with collapse id d2
    P-->>W: 200 OK
    W->>R: Mark d2 sent
```

The first job is a redelivery of work that had already been sent before the worker crashed; the claim check finds it and skips. The second is new, so the worker claims it, sends, and marks it sent. The remaining gap is a crash between the provider's 200 and "mark sent": the claim then says `sending`, and the retry policy must decide whether to resend (risking a duplicate) or wait for the provider receipt. Say this out loud; it shows you know exactly-once to an external system is not achievable, only "effectively once" in the common case.

### 4. Preferences, quiet hours and frequency caps (correctness under load)

**Problem:** every delivery needs the user's preferences, contact points and recent send counts. At 100k deliveries/s that is a heavy read load on a small table, and an opt-out must stick within a minute.

- **Bad: check preferences once in the API.** A scheduled or slow bulk send may go out hours after the user opted out.
- **Good: check at render time, as late as possible**, in the fan-out worker, through a user-ID cache with a short TTL (30–60 s) and explicit invalidation on update. Re-check the policy in the channel worker just before sending if a job has waited in a queue; an earlier render-time check cannot protect an opt-out made during that wait. Read the primary database for the user's own settings page so they see their edit immediately.
- **Great: separate policy from mechanism.** Encode rules per category: `security` ignores opt-outs and quiet hours; `marketing` requires explicit opt-in where the law demands it and honours one-click unsubscribe from email headers. Quiet hours do not drop a notification; they reschedule it into a delay queue keyed by the user's local time. Frequency caps use per-user, per-category counters with a sliding window (`INCR` with expiry in Redis); over-cap bulk messages are dropped or digested, transactional ones are never capped.

Contact points also need hygiene. When APNs answers `410 Unregistered` or FCM returns `UNREGISTERED`, delete the device token; when an email hard-bounces or is marked as spam, suppress the address. Ignoring these hurts sender reputation, and email providers throttle or block senders with high bounce rates.

### 5. Tracking 1 billion deliveries a day (delivery log)

Store attempts in a wide-column store partitioned by `notification_id` (with clustering by user and channel) so "show me this notification's deliveries" is one partition scan, plus a secondary table keyed by `user_id` and time for support lookups. Rows expire with a TTL after 30 days. Webhooks arrive out of order (a `delivered` can beat our own `sent` write), so treat status as a monotonic state machine (`queued < sent < delivered < opened`, with `failed` and `bounced` terminal) and only apply transitions that move forward. Push the webhook ingester behind a queue so a provider's burst of receipts cannot overload the store.

Opens and clicks are tracked with a tracking pixel and redirecting links for email and with client SDK callbacks for push; treat them as analytics events, eventually consistent and lossy under failure, not as part of the delivery guarantee.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a working pipeline with a queue between accept and send, separate channel workers, templates, preference checks and retries. Clear API with 202 and an idempotency key.
- **Senior:** drives the deep dives without prompting: priority isolation that extends to provider quotas, dedupe with deterministic delivery ids, circuit breakers and failover, preference checks at send time, and a delivery log sized for the write volume. Quantifies the broadcast fan-out time.
- **Staff:** frames the platform as shared infrastructure: per-sender quotas and category allow-lists, cost controls on SMS, compliance (consent, unsubscribe, data retention), operational levers (pause a campaign, drain a DLQ, shift provider weights), and the explicit duplicate-versus-loss trade-off at the provider boundary.

## Common mistakes

- Calling providers synchronously from the API, so provider latency and outages leak into every caller.
- A single queue for all priorities, or separate queues that still share one unreserved provider quota.
- Claiming exactly-once delivery to the user's phone.
- Checking preferences only at request time, so delayed sends ignore a recent opt-out.
- Treating a 50M-user broadcast as a loop inside one request instead of a chunked, resumable, throttled job.
- Storing a billion daily status rows in the same relational database as preferences with no retention plan.
- Forgetting token and address hygiene, which quietly degrades deliverability.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] The API returns 202 only after the request is durably stored or enqueued, and it is idempotent.
- [ ] Transactional traffic has its own topic, workers and reserved provider capacity.
- [ ] Every delivery has a deterministic id that dedupes queue redeliveries and retries.
- [ ] Retries use backoff with jitter and end in a dead-letter queue.
- [ ] Email/SMS have a secondary provider behind a circuit breaker; push failures fall back to another channel when it matters.
- [ ] Preferences, quiet hours and frequency caps are checked at send time with a bounded staleness window.
- [ ] Broadcasts are chunked, checkpointed, paced and cancellable.
- [ ] Delivery status is a forward-only state machine in a store sized for ~500 GB/day with TTLs.

## Further reading

- [Firebase Cloud Messaging documentation](https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging)

keyTakeaways: Return 202 only when the request is durable. A queue separates accepting the notification from calling a provider.
Keep urgent messages moving with separate topics, separate workers and reserved provider quota. A priority field cannot reorder one FIFO queue.
Use deterministic delivery IDs and claim before sending to make normal retries and redeliveries effectively once. They cannot guarantee exactly-once delivery to an external provider.
Check preferences, quiet hours and frequency caps as late as possible. Put a clear bound on how long an opt-out can remain unseen.
Run broadcasts as chunked, checkpointed and paced jobs. Choose channels with SMS cost and provider limits in mind.
